title: String tools and string problems
overview: Module 6 practises the `string` class on real judge problems: constructors, range-based loops, `sort` and `reverse` on strings, member functions inside classes, copying heap objects, and classic tasks like palindromes, counting letters, replacing a word and reversing words.

concepts.explain: Build a string from text, part of text, part of another string, or repeated characters.
`for (char c : s)` loops over every element without an index.
Functions inside a class that work with that object's own fields.
`s[i] - 'a'` or `s[i] - 'A'` maps letters to array indices 0-25.
Compare from both ends toward the middle - the classic palindrome check.
Copy field values (or `*a = *b`), not pointers; never read an object after `delete`.

files.title: Ways to construct a string
files.what: Shows the common `string` constructors: from text, from the first n characters, from a position of another string, and n copies of a character.
steps: `string s("Hello")` and `string s2 = "Hello"` are the same.
`string s3("Hello", 3)` keeps the first 3 characters.
`string s4(s, 2)` copies `s` starting at index 2.
`string s5(5, 'a')` repeats `a` five times.

files.title: Range-based for loop
files.what: `for (char c : s)` visits every character of the string without an index.
steps: Read a word `s`.
`for (char c : s)` gives each character in turn.
Print it followed by a space.
files.output_note: `coder` prints as `c o d e r `.

check.q: How do you change the characters inside a range-based loop?

files.title: Sorting the characters of a string
files.what: `sort(s.begin(), s.end())` puts the characters in alphabetical (ASCII) order.
steps: Read `s` and print it.
Sort the whole range from `begin()` to `end()`.
Print the sorted string.

check.q: Where would capital letters go after sorting a mixed string?
check.a: Before lowercase letters, because their ASCII codes are smaller.

files.title: reverse() for arrays and strings
files.what: Uses `reverse(a, a+n)` on an array and `reverse(s.begin(), s.end())` on a string instead of a manual two-pointer swap.
steps: Read `n` numbers into `a`.
`reverse(a, a+n)` flips the array in place.
Print it.
Read a word and reverse it with iterators.
files.input_note: n, the n numbers, then one word.
files.output_note: The program does not compile: `reverse` was not declared, so there is no output. With the fix you would see `5 4 3 2 1 Now, we will reverse the string` and then `olleh`.
files.watch_out: `#include <algorithm>` is missing, so the compiler reports "'reverse' was not declared in this scope". Add that include. Also add `cout << endl;` after the array so the message starts on a new line.

files.title: Member functions
files.what: A class can hold functions too. `hello()` uses the object's own fields to print a greeting and the total marks.
steps: The constructor fills `name`, `roll`, `math`, `english`.
`void hello()` prints the name and `math + english`.
`shammunul.hello()` and `milon.hello()` each use their own data.
files.output_note: For Shammunul: total `184` (99 + 85). For Milon: total `156` (85 + 71).

check.q: Inside `hello()`, why can you write `name` without an object in front?
check.a: A member function runs on the object it was called on, so `name` means `this->name`.

files.title: Copying dynamic objects (and a use-after-delete)
files.what: Copies fields from one heap object to another, then shows that `*kohli3 = *dhoni3` copies all fields at once.
steps: Create heap objects `dhoni` (100) and `kohli` (13) and print them.
Copy `country` and `jersy` from dhoni into kohli, then `delete dhoni`.
kohli still shows 100 - it owns its own copy.
The code then builds `kohli2` from `dhoni`'s fields after dhoni was deleted.
The last part copies whole objects with `*kohli3 = *dhoni3`.
files.output_note: The first three lines are right (`Dhoni is 100`, `Kohli is 13`, `Kohli is 100`). Then the program crashes (status `exit_0xc0000005`, access violation) and the rest never prints.
files.watch_out: `new Cricketer(dhoni->country, ...)` reads `dhoni` after `delete dhoni` - use-after-free. Create `kohli2` before deleting dhoni (or from `kohli`). `dhoni3` is also used correctly only because it is deleted after the copy.

check.a: Every field of the object (country, name and jersy), so kohli3's name becomes Dhoni too.

files.title: Palindrome (two pointers)
files.what: Moves `left` and `right` pointers toward each other and stops at the first mismatch.
steps: `left = 0`, `right = s.size() - 1`.
While `left < right`, compare `s[left]` and `s[right]`.
A mismatch means NO; otherwise move both inward.
If the loop ends, it is a palindrome.

check.a: When they meet at the middle character, it matches itself, so there is nothing left to check.

files.title: Palindrome (using reverse)
files.what: Makes a reversed copy with `reverse` and compares it with the original.
steps: Copy `s` into `rev_s`.
`reverse(rev_s.begin(), rev_s.end())`.
`s == rev_s` means palindrome.

check.q: What extra cost does this version have over the two-pointer one?
check.a: It uses O(n) extra memory for the reversed copy.

files.title: New Words (how many EGYPT)
files.what: Counts how many times each letter of EGYPT appears (ignoring case); the answer is the smallest of those counts.
steps: Turn capital letters into small ones with `s[i] - 'A' + 'a'`.
Count `e`, `g`, `y`, `p`, `t`.
Each word needs one of each, so the answer is the minimum count.
files.output_note: `pemigdbeigyypetet` prints `2`: g and y appear twice, the others at least twice.

check.q: If a string has 5 e's, 3 g's and no t, what is the answer?

files.title: Replace Word (EGYPT to space)
files.what: Scans the string; when the next 5 letters are EGYPT it adds a space and jumps 5, otherwise copies one letter.
steps: `i` walks through `s`.
`s.substr(i, 5) == "EGYPT"` checks for the word (only if 5 letters remain).
Match: add `' '` and `i += 5`.
No match: add `s[i]` and `i++`.
files.output_note: `ITALYEGYPTEGYPTZ` becomes `ITALY  Z` - two spaces for the two EGYPTs.

check.q: Why jump by 5 after a match?
check.a: So the letters of the replaced word are not copied or matched again.

files.title: Reverse Words
files.what: Splits the line with `stringstream`, reverses words, and prints them with single spaces and no trailing space.
steps: `getline` reads the whole line; `stringstream ss(s)` splits it.
The first word is read and printed without a leading space.
Every later word is reversed with `reverse` and printed after a space.
files.output_note: `hello world abc` prints `hello dlrow cba` - the first word was not reversed.
files.watch_out: The first word is printed without calling `reverse`, so it stays unchanged (the task reverses every word). Add `reverse(word.begin(), word.end());` right after the first `ss >> word;`.

check.q: How do you print words separated by spaces without a trailing space?
check.a: Print the first word alone, then print `" " + word` for each remaining word.

files.title: Lucky? (ticket digits)
files.what: A six-digit ticket is lucky when the first three digits add up to the same value as the last three.
steps: Read each ticket as a string so leading zeros stay.
Turn each char into a digit with `num[i] - '0'`.
Compare the two sums; store YES/NO and print all at the end.

check.q: Why read the ticket as a string instead of an int?
check.a: An int would lose leading zeros like in `045207`, and digit access is easier on a string.

files.title: ICPC Balloons
files.what: Each solve gives 1 balloon, and the first solve of a problem gives 1 extra. A `bool` array of size 26 remembers which problems were already solved.
steps: For each test reset `first_time[26]` to false.
For each letter add 1.
If this letter was not seen before, add 1 more and mark it.
Store the total; print all results at the end.
files.complexity: Time O(n) per test · Space O(26)
files.input_note: t; then for each test n and the string.

check.a: It turns a letter A-Z into an index 0-25 for the `first_time` array.

recap: `for (char c : s)` reads; `for (char &c : s)` can modify.
Map letters to 0-25 with `c - 'a'` for counting.
Palindrome: two pointers (O(1) memory) or compare with a reversed copy.

check_yourself.q: How do you count how many times a word can be built from a string's letters?
check_yourself.a: Count each needed letter and take the minimum (divided by how many times the word needs that letter).

check_yourself.q: What goes wrong when you use a pointer after `delete`?
check_yourself.a: Undefined behaviour - the memory may be reused, giving garbage or a crash.
